Nuclear Weapons. Nuclear weapons are explosive devices whose destructive power derives from atomic fission or fusion reactions, capable of destroying cities and killing millions. Developed in secret during World War II and deployed against Japan in August 1945, they inaugurated an era of unprecedented military and strategic power. Nuclear weapons transformed international relations, deterrence theory, and the calculus of war by introducing the possibility of civilizational annihilation.

Two types exist. Fission or atomic bombs derive energy from uranium-235 or plutonium-239 splitting. Fusion or thermonuclear bombs derive energy from hydrogen isotope fusion and are many times more powerful. The atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima on August sixth, 1945 and Nagasaki on August ninth, 1945 killed approximately two hundred thousand people instantly and through radiation and burn injuries in the following weeks, including many civilians. A single bomb destroyed an entire city, introduced radiation sickness and long-term health consequences, and raised moral and strategic questions that persist.

During the Cold War, both superpowers acquired thousands of warheads and delivery systems including missiles, bombers, and submarines, creating arsenals capable of destroying human civilization multiple times over. Nuclear weapons changed military strategy by making warfare between nuclear powers existentially risky. Conventional wars persisted, but superpowers avoided direct military conflict, instead fighting through proxy wars. Proliferation concerns emerged as more nations acquired weapons: the Soviet Union in 1949, Britain in 1952, France in 1960, China in 1964, and others, complicating international security and deterrence calculations.
